title: Fusillade warmup probe — microburst priming log
content:
Context:
This is a personal scratchpad for a targeted warmup/warm-cache experiment we ran to understand fusillade-style microbursts: many small concurrent requests hitting an instance with a cold KV cache and partially primed attention cache. Goal: quantify priming time, transient p99 behavior, and whether lightweight prefix-cache seeding (synthetic warmups) measurably reduces tail under tight SLOs.

Hypothesis:
- Short synthetic priming (30s of controlled traffic) reduces p99 by ~15-30% during a subsequent 60s fusillade compared to no priming.
- Cost of priming (extra tokens) is ~0.5–1.5% of baseline token spend for a typical burst profile; acceptable trade for p99 improvements.

Environment:
- Model: mix of Llama-2-13B (FP16) and a quantized 7B variant for quick A/B.
- Hardware: single A100-40GB (dev fleet slice), CUDA 12.1, cudnn 9.3, kernel 6.x (container image: redwood/runtime:canary-2025-11)
- Runtime flags: --continuous-batching=on --kv-cache-mode=on --eviction-policy=LRU --batch-window-ms=8
- Client harness: custom Go harness (repo: linked PR above) + k6 for synthetic waveform generation

Traffic profile (fusillade):
- Burst window: 60s (main), preceded by optional priming window: 30s
- Arrival shape: compound Poisson with lambda peak at 420 qps for 5s pulses within the fusillade; average across 60s ~110 qps
- Payloads: average tokens/request ~45 (prompt + short gen), typical context lengths: 1–3 prompt turns
- Concurrency config on instance: max_concurrency=32, queue_depth=128

Test matrix (important runs):
1) baseline (cold start, no priming) — run A
2) short priming (synthetic prefix seeds for 30s at 60 qps, then fusillade) — run B
3) aggressive priming (full-token replay: 30s at 200 qps) — run C
4) quantized 7B baseline (cold, no priming) — run D
5) quantized 7B short priming — run E

Instrumentation captured:
- client-side latency histogram (0–3s buckets), per-request metadata: model_variant, batch_size, gpu_mem_snapshot, kv_cache_hit:true/false
- server-side trace IDs and batch sizes, token generation rate, batch assembly time
- GPU metrics: SM utilization, memory alloc delta, PCIe copies, kernel durations (approx from NVTX)

Quick raw observations (numbers are medians over 3 runs unless noted):
- Run A (13B, cold): p50=48ms, p95=220ms, p99=480ms, max=1.8s, throughput observed stable ~108 qps overall but heavy tail during peaks
- Run B (13B, short priming): p50=46ms, p95=185ms, p99=360ms, max=1.2s — ~25% improvement on p99 vs run A
- Run C (13B, aggressive priming): p50=45ms, p95=170ms, p99=340ms, max=950ms — marginal gains vs B for large token cost
- Run D (7B-q, cold): p50=32ms, p95=140ms, p99=310ms, max=1.1s — overall lower absolute but similar relative tail shape
- Run E (7B-q, short priming): p50=30ms, p95=118ms, p99=240ms, max=720ms

Ascii sparkline (p99 across time windows, run A vs B):
- run A p99 trend:  ▂▁▁▁▂▃▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▆▅▃▂
- run B p99 trend:  ▂▁▁▁▂▂▃▅▅▅▆▅▃▂
(Visual is rough: primed runs avoid the sustained high p99 plateau in the middle 20s of fusillade)

Observations + possible root causes:
- KV-cache priming matters for repeated context tokens; when priming contains representative prefixes we see lower batch assembly time and fewer single-request batches during the peak.
- Batch assembly time dominates p95->p99 during short, punchy pulses: when the runtime cannot coalesce into 2–4 request batches because requests are slightly out-of-sync, per-request overhead & kernel startup inflate the tail.
- Aggressive priming reduces tail further but with diminishing returns: token cost grows, and kernel cache (cuBLAS/cuDNN) cold misses become less significant after small priming window.
- Quantized models show proportionally similar gains; priming is still effective and cheaper token-wise.

Notes on measurement noise and caveats:
- Single-A100 results vary vs multi-GPU slices; cross-instance network jitter adds noise to p99 (we isolated experiment to one machine though).
- We didn't fully isolate background housekeeping (GC, trace exporter batching) — saw correlated spikes at ~45s in a couple runs (likely exporter flush).
- The harness' arrival jitter has micro-timing variance; recommend re-running with client-side aligned clock and tighter send scheduling for verification.

Action items (next runs):
- A: repeat B and E with exporter disabled + NVTX full tracing to confirm whether observed mid-run spike is exporter-related (owner: Kendall, priority: P1)
- B: add a priming pattern generator that uses sampled real prompts from prod anonymized set (to test representativeness vs synthetic short tokens)
- C: evaluate lighter-weight priming: seed only top-K tokens per layer (experiment with K=4,8) — measure token cost vs p99 benefit
- D: run same matrix on dedicated-node (multi-GPU slice) to see inter-GPU batch coalescing effect

Quick heuristics for productization (brain dump):
- For Dedicated customers with strict p99 SLOs, offer an "auto-priming" option: short, low-rate prefix seeding triggered at first sign of a surge (cost budget per-hour).
- Provide SDK helper to generate representative seeds from historical prompts to maximize priming ROI.
- In Console, surface an "expected p99 delta" estimate when enabling priming (based on historical runs and config).

Misc scratchnotes (todo later):
- compute token-cost estimate per 1M bursts for each priming policy (rough back-of-envelope: short priming @60 qps for 30s -> 108k requests * 45 tokens ~= 4.86M tokens; cost delta depends on pricing model)
- check whether --batch-window-ms=8 vs 4 provides better tradeoff during primed runs (microbench)
- follow up with SRE on queue_depth=128 limits and whether request rejections occurred in any runs (saw 2 early drops in run A logs)

Conclusions (working):
- Short, representative priming materially reduces p99 in fusillade-style bursts (observed ~20–30% improvement on 13B); returns diminish with heavier priming.
- Priming is a promising product-level lever for SLO-sensitive customers; must be paired with representative seed selection and cost guardrails.

End notes: capture raw histograms + NVTX traces uploaded to artifact storage under: /artifacts/warmup-probe/fusillade-2025-11 (link in linked_artifacts once available).
